concepts.title: Law of Conservation of Mass
concepts.definition: A fundamental chemical principle stating that the total mass of substances participating in a chemical reaction remains constant, meaning matter is neither created nor destroyed.
concepts.key_idea: The total mass before a chemical reaction equals the total mass after the reaction.
question_patterns: verify whether the Law of Conservation of Mass is obeyed
calculate the mass of product formed when reactants of known masses combine
find the missing mass of a reactant or product in a closed system
how much water is formed according to the Law of Conservation of Mass
compute the answer step by step for law of conservation of mass

solution_steps.action: Calculate the total mass of the reactants
solution_steps.explain: Sum the masses of all starting substances (reactants).

solution_steps.action: Calculate the total mass of the known products
solution_steps.explain: Sum the masses of all known products formed in the reaction.

solution_steps.action: Determine the mass of the missing product or reactant
solution_steps.explain: Subtract the total known products from the total reactants to find the missing mass.

concepts.title: Law of Constant Proportions
concepts.definition: A chemical law stating that a given chemical compound always contains its component elements in a fixed and definite ratio by mass, regardless of its source or preparation method.
concepts.key_idea: Elements in a pure chemical compound are always combined in a constant mass ratio.
question_patterns: how much of element B is needed to react completely with a given mass of element A
find the mass of compound produced from a given mass of element
what mass of oxygen must be present to satisfy the Law of Constant Proportions
calculate the mass of chlorine required to react with sodium
find the required value in a law of constant proportions problem

solution_steps.action: Calculate the mass of the second element required
solution_steps.explain: Multiply the given mass of the first element by the ratio of the second element to the first.

solution_steps.action: Calculate the total mass of the compound formed
solution_steps.explain: Sum the masses of both combining elements to get the total compound mass.

solution_steps.action: Verify the constant mass ratio is preserved
solution_steps.explain: Confirm that the ratio mass_b/mass_a equals the fixed ratio_b/ratio_a, validating the Law of Constant Proportions.

concepts.title: Dalton's Atomic Theory
concepts.definition: A set of postulates proposing that all matter is made up of small, indivisible particles called atoms, which are identical for a given element and combine in simple whole-number ratios to form compounds.
concepts.key_idea: Matter is made up of indivisible atoms that rearrange during chemical reactions without being created or destroyed.
question_patterns: what are the postulates of Dalton's atomic theory
which postulate of Dalton's atomic theory is the result of the law of conservation of mass
explain how Dalton's theory explains the law of definite proportions
state Dalton's assumptions about atoms of different elements
justify why dalton's atomic theory matters

solution_steps.action: Identify the relevant postulate of Dalton's Atomic Theory
solution_steps.explain: Match the observed chemical behavior (e.g., mass conservation or constant proportions) to the corresponding postulate.

solution_steps.action: Verify the property or law
solution_steps.explain: Explain how the indivisibility of atoms or their combination in simple whole-number ratios justifies the chemical law.

solution_steps.action: Conclude the justification
solution_steps.explain: State how the matched postulate accounts for the observed chemical behavior, confirming that Dalton's theory explains the law.

concepts.title: Covalent Bonding
concepts.definition: A chemical bond formed when two atoms share one or more pairs of valence electrons to reach a stable, filled outer shell configuration.
concepts.key_idea: Non-metal atoms share electrons to complete their octet or duplet and form stable molecules.
question_patterns: explain the formation of a covalent bond in a molecule
draw the structure of the nitrogen molecule
explain the formation of the fluorine molecule
how do atoms share electrons to form a water molecule
short note on covalent bonding

solution_steps.action: Write the electronic configuration of the combining atoms
solution_steps.explain: Determine the number of valence electrons for each atom using its atomic number.

solution_steps.action: Determine the number of shared electron pairs
solution_steps.explain: Calculate how many electrons each atom needs to complete its valence shell (octet or duplet).

solution_steps.action: Represent the covalent bond
solution_steps.explain: Show the shared pairs of electrons as single, double, or triple bonds between the atoms.

concepts.title: Ionic Bonding
concepts.definition: A chemical bond formed by the complete transfer of one or more valence electrons from a metal atom to a non-metal atom, resulting in oppositely charged ions held together by electrostatic attraction.
concepts.key_idea: Metals lose electrons to form cations, and non-metals gain electrons to form anions, which attract each other.
question_patterns: explain the formation of an ionic bond in sodium chloride
what kind of ion will oxygen form
illustrate how sodium sulfide is formed
show the formation of cations of potassium and calcium
give one everyday example of ionic bonding

solution_steps.action: Identify electron loss to form a cation
solution_steps.explain: The metal atom loses valence electrons to achieve a stable octet, forming a positively charged cation.

solution_steps.action: Identify electron gain to form an anion
solution_steps.explain: The non-metal atom gains the transferred electrons to complete its octet, forming a negatively charged anion.

solution_steps.action: Represent the electrostatic attraction
solution_steps.explain: Show the oppositely charged ions attracting each other to form a neutral ionic compound.

concepts.title: Writing Chemical Formulae
concepts.definition: The process of determining the symbolic representation of a compound by crossing over the valencies or charges of its constituent ions or elements to find their simplest neutral ratio.
concepts.key_idea: The criss-cross method balances both positive and negative charges to yield a neutral chemical formula.
question_patterns: write the formula for sodium hydrogencarbonate
write the formula for ferric chloride
derive the formula of aluminium sulfate
write the formula for magnesium hydroxide
why is writing chemical formulae important

solution_steps.action: Write symbols and valencies
solution_steps.explain: Write the symbol of the cation (or less electronegative element) first, followed by the anion, with their respective valencies or charges below them.

solution_steps.action: Criss-cross the valencies
solution_steps.explain: Cross over the valencies to write them as subscripts for the opposite elements.

solution_steps.action: Simplify to the simplest ratio
solution_steps.explain: Divide the subscripts by their greatest common divisor to get the simplest whole-number ratio, and use brackets for polyatomic ions if their subscript is greater than one.

concepts.title: Molecular Mass of Covalent Compounds
concepts.definition: For a covalent molecule, add up the atomic masses of every atom in one molecule; the total comes in unified atomic mass units (u).
concepts.key_idea: Add up the atomic masses of all individual atoms in the molecular formula.
question_patterns: find the molecular mass of nitric acid
find the molecular mass of methane
calculate the molecular mass of water
what is the molecular mass of carbon dioxide
compute the answer step by step for molecular mass of covalent compounds

solution_steps.action: Calculate the mass contribution of the first element
solution_steps.explain: Multiply the number of atoms of the first element by its atomic mass.

solution_steps.action: Calculate the mass contribution of the second element
solution_steps.explain: Multiply the number of atoms of the second element by its atomic mass.

solution_steps.action: Calculate the mass contribution of the third element
solution_steps.explain: Multiply the number of atoms of the third element by its atomic mass.

solution_steps.action: Sum the contributions to find the total molecular mass
solution_steps.explain: Add all the individual element mass contributions together.

concepts.title: Formula Unit Mass of Ionic Compounds
concepts.definition: For an ionic compound, the atomic masses are totaled over its simplest formula unit instead of a molecule.
concepts.key_idea: Since ionic compounds do indeed not have discrete molecules, their mass is calculated using the formula unit.
question_patterns: find the formula unit mass of potassium chloride
find the formula unit mass of magnesium hydroxide
calculate the formula unit mass of sodium oxide
determine the formula unit mass of calcium nitrate
what is the result in this formula unit mass of ionic compounds problem

solution_steps.action: Calculate the mass contribution of the first ion/element
solution_steps.explain: Multiply the count of the first element in the formula unit by its atomic mass.

solution_steps.action: Calculate the mass contribution of the second ion/element
solution_steps.explain: Multiply the count of the second element in the formula unit by its atomic mass.

solution_steps.action: Calculate the mass contribution of the third ion/element
solution_steps.explain: Multiply the count of the third element in the formula unit by its atomic mass.

solution_steps.action: Sum the contributions to find the formula unit mass
solution_steps.explain: Add all the element mass contributions together to get the total formula unit mass.

concepts.title: Properties of Ionic and Covalent Compounds
concepts.definition: The characteristic physical behaviors (solubility, electrical conductivity, both melting and boiling points) that distinguish ionic compounds from covalent compounds using their bonding nature.
concepts.key_idea: Strong electrostatic forces in ionic compounds vs. weaker intermolecular forces in covalent compounds govern their physical properties.
question_patterns: what type of chemical bond is present in a solid compound that conducts electricity when dissolved
predict the electrical conductivity of its aqueous solution
compare the solubility of ionic and covalent compounds
why do covalent compounds have low melting and boiling points
list the main features of properties of ionic and covalent compounds

solution_steps.action: Identify the bonding type
solution_steps.explain: Determine if the compound is ionic (metal and non-metal) or covalent (non-metals only).

solution_steps.action: Analyze the physical property
solution_steps.explain: Relate the property (e.g., conductivity, solubility, melting point) to the presence of free ions or the strength of intermolecular forces.

solution_steps.action: Conclude the classification
solution_steps.explain: State the final classification of the compound as ionic or covalent based on the observed physical property.

questions: A particular element (A) has one electron in its third shell. There is another element (B) with six electrons in its second shell. (i) How many electrons does A tend to give or take to become stable? (ii) What kind of ion would it form? (iii) How many electrons does B tend to give or take to become stable? (iv) What kind of ion would it form? (v) If A and B were to combine, what kind of bond would be formed? (vi) What would be the formula for the compound thus formed?

An element X has six electrons in its outer shell and forms a diatomic molecule. (i) Why would that be so? (ii) What kind of bond would it form? (iii) Draw the structure of the molecule it would form. (iv) A certain other element Y has two electrons in its second shell. Draw the structure of the molecule that X would form with Y.

Choose the correct statement(s) and correct the false statement(s): (i) Elements are made up of molecules and compounds are made up of atoms. (ii) The molecule of a compound is always made up of two or more atoms of the same kind. (iii) One molecule of nitrogen gas contains three nitrogen atoms. (iv) Water is made of two hydrogen atoms, covalently bonded with one oxygen atom.

(ii) Phosphoric acid (H3PO4), used to make phosphate fertiliser and detergents. (iii) Sodium hydrogencarbonate (NaHCO3), used to relieve acidity and helps in digestion.

Complete the table by writing the formulae of the compounds formed by the cations on the left (Li+, Al3+, Cu2+) and the anions at the top (NO3-, SO42-, PO43-, NH4+).

If a species has 11 protons, 12 neutrons and 10 electrons then: (i) what is its atomic number and mass number? (ii) is it neutral, a cation or an anion? Explain. (iii) write its electronic configuration. (iv) name the species.

Two elements, A and B, have the following configurations: A: 2, 8, 5; B: 2, 8, 7. (i) Which element is more reactive? (ii) Will A and B form ionic or covalent bonds when they combine? Explain using electron transfer or sharing. (iii) Predict the formula of the compound they would form.

Reason (R): Copper and sulfate ions are fixed in the lattice in molten state, while in solid state they can move freely. Choose the correct option: (i) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. (ii) Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. (iii) A is true, but R is false. (iv) A is false, but R is true.
